client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work. They just handed me this massive project with an insane deadline, and half my team is out, so I'm basically trying to do the work of three people. I don't know if talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling stretched thin with so much pressure coming from all sides. I'm glad you decided to give this a shot — even if you're not sure it'll help, just putting words to what's going on can sometimes start to shift things a little. I'm curious, when you think about everything piling up, what feels like the *most* overwhelming part of it all?

client: Honestly, the most overwhelming part is just feeling like I'm completely alone in all of it. Like, I have people around me, technically, but none of them really get what's going on inside my head, and trying to explain it just feels exhausting. So I end up saying nothing, and then the loneliness gets even worse.
therapist: That sense of being surrounded by people yet still feeling completely alone is such a painful and isolating experience, and it takes real courage to name it. It sounds like there's almost a cycle happening — you hold back to avoid the effort of explaining, but then the silence leaves you feeling even more disconnected. What do you think gets in the way most when you consider opening up to someone — is it more about not wanting to burden them, or something else?

client: I think it's more than just not wanting to burden them — it's also this fear that even if I do open up, they still won't really get it. Like I'll go through all that effort of being vulnerable and they'll just say something generic like "oh everyone feels that way sometimes" and I'll feel even more alone than before. So it almost feels safer to just stay quiet and protect myself from that disappointment.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — you've probably had enough experiences of reaching out and feeling unseen that your mind has learned to protect you by not even trying. In CBT we'd call that a kind of protective belief, and while it keeps you safe from disappointment, it also keeps you locked out of the connection you're actually craving. I'm wondering — has there ever been a moment, even a small one, where someone *did* respond in a way that felt genuinely understanding?

client: I have to think about that for a second... there was this one time a few months ago when I texted my friend Maya after a really bad night, and she actually called me back instead of just sending a quick reply. It felt good in the moment, but then I kind of talked myself out of it, like maybe she only did it because she felt obligated or something. I guess I'm not sure I can trust that one moment to mean much when most of the time I still feel like people are just going through the motions with me.
therapist: It's really meaningful that Maya's response came to mind — and it's worth noticing that your mind quickly moved to explain it away, almost like it couldn't quite let that moment of genuine connection land. That's such a common pattern — when we're used to disappointment, our brain can actually work *against* us by discounting the evidence that contradicts our fears. What do you think it would mean for you if Maya's call *wasn't* out of obligation — if she just genuinely cared?

client: I mean... if she genuinely cared, that would be... I don't know, it almost feels scarier than if it were obligation, honestly. Because then I'd have to actually believe I'm worth caring about, and that's a much harder thing to sit with. It's easier to assume people are just being polite than to risk actually trusting that and then being wrong later.
therapist: What you just said is really profound — that believing you're worth caring about feels *scarier* than the alternative, because it opens you up to a loss that would actually mean something. That tells me this isn't really about Maya or anyone else at its core; it's about a much deeper belief you carry about your own worthiness of love and connection. I'd gently ask — where do you think that belief that you might *not* be worth caring about first came from?

client: I sat with that question for a second because it kind of hit me harder than I expected. I think... honestly, it probably goes back to my dad. He was just never really there emotionally, and when I did try to connect with him, it always felt like I was bothering him or asking for too much.
therapist: That took real courage to sit with and share, and it makes so much sense that this is where it begins — when the first person who was supposed to show you that you mattered made you feel like a burden instead, of course that became the lens you learned to see yourself through. The little version of you drew the most logical conclusion available at the time: *I must be asking for too much.* I'm wondering, when you look back at that child reaching out to his dad — do you think he was actually asking for too much?

client: No, I don't think he was asking for too much. He just wanted his dad to show up, to actually be there, and that's... that's not a big ask, is it? But even saying that out loud, there's this part of me that immediately wants to argue back against it, like some reflex that says "yeah, but maybe you were too needy, maybe you were difficult."
therapist: No, it really isn't a big ask — wanting your dad to show up emotionally is one of the most fundamental human needs a child can have, and you deserved that. What's so important to notice is exactly what you just caught in real time — that reflexive voice that rushes in to call you "too needy" whenever you get close to giving yourself something true and compassionate. That voice sounds like it's been around a long time, and I'm curious — whose voice does it actually sound like when you hear it?

client: It sounds like my dad's voice, honestly. Like, I can almost hear him saying "stop being so sensitive" or "you're making a big deal out of nothing" whenever I'd try to bring something up with him. And the worst part is, I don't even know if he meant it to hurt me — I think he genuinely believed he was toughening me up or something, which somehow makes it harder to be angry about it.
therapist: It's such a painful and complicated place to be — holding hurt toward someone who may not have even known they were causing it, because that can make the anger feel somehow unfair or unjustified, even when the wound is completely real. But here's something worth sitting with: the impact of those words on you doesn't require him to have intended the harm — "stop being so sensitive" still taught you that your feelings were a problem, regardless of what he meant by it. How do you feel about the idea that you're allowed to grieve what you didn't get from him, even without needing to cast him as a villain?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept that... but it feels almost too convenient, like I'm giving myself permission to feel sad about something I should just be over by now. Like, if I start grieving what I didn't get, doesn't that mean I'm blaming him anyway, just in a softer way? I guess I'm not sure I know how to grieve something without it turning into resentment.
therapist: There's something really worth gently challenging in what you just said — the idea that you "should be over it by now" is actually that same old voice again, telling you your feelings are too much or taking up too much space. Grief and blame are actually quite different things — grief is about *you* and what you needed, while blame is about him and what he did wrong, and you can fully do one without the other. I'm wondering, what would it look like to mourn the emotionally present dad you deserved, not as an accusation toward him, but as an act of kindness toward yourself?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept that distinction between grief and blame... but honestly, it feels kind of blurry to me in practice. Like, when I start to feel sad about not having the dad I needed, it almost immediately tips into anger at him for not being there, and then I feel guilty for being angry. I guess I'm not sure I actually know how to do one without the other sliding in.
therapist: What you're describing — sadness sliding into anger, then guilt rushing in to shut it all down — is actually a really common emotional loop, and it makes sense that it feels blurry because those feelings are genuinely tangled together, especially when the loss is tied to someone you also love. The guilt about the anger is worth paying attention to, because it might be another way that old voice keeps you from fully feeling anything — like even your emotions have to be policed before they get too big. I'm curious, when the anger toward your dad shows up, what does that guilty voice tell you about what it means to feel angry at him?
